quiz.q: What do you own when you buy a share?
quiz.why: A share is a piece of ownership: you become a shareholder, not a lender.
opts: A loan made to the company
A piece of ownership in the company

title: What is a share?
examples: With 0.45 of an Nvidia share, you own a small piece of every chip sold, every patent filed, every data centre equipped.
If Nvidia doubles in value, your 0.45 share is worth twice as much — without you having to do anything.
paragraphs: A share is a piece of ownership in a company. Holding one, even a fraction of one, makes you a shareholder: a part-owner.
If the company creates value, your share can gain value too. If it loses value, your share can fall. That is what risk means.

quiz.q: Where does a dividend come from?
quiz.why: A dividend is a slice of the company's profits paid out to shareholders.

title: Dividends
examples: Air Liquide pays a dividend of roughly 2.9% a year. With 0.21 of a share, you will receive your first slice of profits next May.
A company that pays out 40% of its profits as a dividend keeps the other 60% to invest in its own growth.
paragraphs: Some companies hand part of their profits back to their shareholders: that is the dividend, usually paid quarterly or once a year.
Not all of them do. Fast-growing companies would rather reinvest their profits.

quiz.q: Why diversify a portfolio?
quiz.why: Spreading your investment reduces the impact of any single fall.

title: Diversification
examples: Nvidia (tech, United States) plus Air Liquide (industry, France): two very different engines. That is already the beginning of diversification.
A portfolio concentrated in a single stock can lose 50% in a day; spread across ten stocks, one collapse is cushioned.
paragraphs: Putting every egg in one basket is risky. Diversifying means spreading your investment across several companies, sectors and countries.
When one falls, another may rise: your portfolio becomes steadier over time.

quiz.q: What does ten years of market history show?
quiz.why: Over long periods, markets have historically rewarded patience.

title: Thinking long term
examples: €100 invested in the world's largest companies in 2014 was worth about €320 ten years later — having lived through two crises.
Selling after a 10% fall to buy back later usually means missing the rebound that follows.
paragraphs: Over a single day, the stock market is unpredictable. Over ten years, markets have historically rewarded patience.
An investor is not a speculator: you do not check your portfolio every hour, you let time do the work.

quiz.q: Why reinvest your gains?
quiz.why: Reinvesting creates a snowball effect: your gains put your gains to work.

title: Compound interest
examples: €25 a month at 7% a year: about €4,300 after 10 years, of which €1,300 comes from interest alone.
Without reinvesting, that same €25 a month would only earn simple interest — roughly €3,000 less over 10 years.
paragraphs: Reinvesting your gains puts the gains themselves to work. It is a snowball effect: slow at first, powerful with time.
The key is not the amount, it is the duration. Start early and do not interrupt.

quiz.q: What does "Nvidia +1.4% today" mean?
quiz.why: The change compares the current price with the previous close.
opts: The stock is worth 1.4% more than yesterday

title: Reading a share price
examples: Nvidia "+1.4% today": the share is worth 1.4% more than at yesterday's close. Nothing more, nothing less.
Heavy trading volume often signals that important news about the company has just been published.
paragraphs: A price reflects where buyers and sellers agree, continuously. It moves because expectations move.
Open, close, volume, change: four numbers are enough to read the essentials.

quiz.q: What does an index like the CAC 40 measure?
quiz.why: An index groups several companies together to reflect the health of a market.
opts: A basket of a market's largest companies

title: Indices: CAC 40 & S&P 500
examples: When people say "the market is up", they usually mean an index — not every stock.
The S&P 500 has risen more than tenfold since 2009, despite several crises along the way.
paragraphs: An index is a basket of shares that measures the health of an entire market.
CAC 40: the 40 largest French companies. S&P 500: the 500 largest American ones.

quiz.q: What are you buying with a share of an S&P 500 ETF?
quiz.why: An ETF replicates a whole index in a single purchase.
opts: A fund that replicates the 500 largest US companies

title: What is an ETF?
examples: An S&P 500 ETF makes you a shareholder in the 500 largest American companies in a single purchase.
A CAC 40 ETF makes you a shareholder in the 40 largest French companies in a single portfolio line.
paragraphs: An ETF is a listed fund that replicates an entire index. One share = hundreds of companies.
It is the simplest diversification tool there is, with very low fees.

quiz.q: What does high volatility mean?
quiz.why: Volatility measures how widely a price swings.

title: Risk and volatility
examples: Nvidia can move 5% in a day; Air Liquide rarely more than 2%. Two profiles, two roles in a portfolio.
A volatile stock is not necessarily a bad one — it simply asks for steadier nerves.
paragraphs: Volatility is how widely a price swings. High volatility means strong emotions.
Risk can be managed: diversification, a long horizon, and only investing money you do not need.

quiz.q: Why are fees "the invisible enemy"?
quiz.why: Every fee charged is return lost, and that return can never be reinvested.
opts: They cut a return that will never compound

title: Fees, the invisible enemy
examples: Withdrawing €50 with a €9.99 fee means losing 20% of the amount. Better to withdraw rarely, and all at once.
Two identical funds charging 0.2% and 1.5% a year can end up thousands of euros apart after 20 years.
paragraphs: Every fee charged is return lost — return that will never compound.
Comparing fees before investing pays off more than hunting for "the right stock".

quiz.q: When are gains taxed in France?
quiz.why: Gains are taxed when you sell, not before.
opts: At the moment of the sale

title: Tax for beginners
examples: Your €12 gain on Nvidia will only be taxed the day you sell.
Holding a stock rather than selling it every year avoids triggering tax each time.
paragraphs: In France, gains are taxed at 30% (the "flat tax") at the moment of the sale — not before.
As long as you do not sell, you pay nothing: the long term is a tax advantage too.

quiz.q: What should a good investment plan contain?
quiz.why: A simple plan comes down to three things: a goal, a regular amount, a time horizon.
opts: A goal, a regular amount, a horizon
Nothing but a large lump sum

title: Building your investment plan
examples: "€25 a month for 10 years to fund my studies": that is a complete plan.
A plan written down in black and white is far easier to stick to than a vague intention to "save better".
paragraphs: A good plan fits in three lines: a goal, a regular amount, a time horizon.
The best plan is the one you will keep to without thinking about it — hence recurring investment.

quiz.q: What is the real difference between a share and a bond?
quiz.why: A shareholder owns a piece of the company; a bondholder has simply lent it money.
opts: A share makes you an owner, a bond makes you a creditor

title: Share or bond?
examples: Lending €1,000 to the French state at 3% a year is a bond: you get your capital back at maturity, plus the interest.
Buying an Nvidia share is a bet on its future growth — with no guaranteed return, but no ceiling either.
paragraphs: A share makes you an owner of a company. A bond makes you its creditor: you lend it money in exchange for fixed interest.
A share can climb far higher… but it can also fall further. A bond is more predictable, with a generally lower return.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of DCA?
quiz.why: Investing regularly means buying at a range of prices, which averages out your entry cost without having to guess the right moment.
opts: Smoothing your average purchase price over time

title: Recurring investment (DCA)
examples: €25 invested in Nvidia every month, whether the price rises or falls: sometimes you buy dear, sometimes cheap — on average, a reasonable price.
An investor who has been waiting for "the right moment" since 2020 has probably missed a rise of more than 150% on world indices.
paragraphs: Dollar-cost averaging means investing the same amount at regular intervals, rather than one large sum at once.
The method smooths your average purchase price over time and removes the pressure of "finding the right moment".

quiz.q: What does the P/E ratio measure?
quiz.why: The P/E ratio compares the share price with the company's annual earnings per share.
opts: The size of the dividend paid
How many years of earnings the share price is worth

title: Understanding the P/E ratio
examples: A €100 share earning €5 a year has a P/E of 20: you are paying 20 times its annual earnings.
Nvidia has historically carried a high P/E because investors are betting on its growth in AI; a mature industrial company will often have a lower one.
paragraphs: The P/E ratio (price-earnings ratio) compares a share's price with its earnings per share. It tells you how many years of earnings you are paying for.
A high P/E means the market expects strong future growth; a low P/E can signal an overlooked stock — or one in trouble.

quiz.q: What does equity represent?
quiz.why: Equity is what would be left for shareholders if the company sold all its assets and repaid all its debts.
opts: The difference between assets and debts
The share price on the market

title: Reading a balance sheet, simply
examples: Air Liquide owns plants and patents worth billions: those are its assets, financed partly by debt and partly by its shareholders.
Debt that far exceeds assets is a warning sign, even when the share price looks attractive.
paragraphs: A balance sheet lists what a company owns (assets) and what it owes (debts). The difference is its equity.
A healthy company generally has more assets than debts, and equity that grows from one year to the next.

quiz.q: Is a company with huge revenue necessarily profitable?
quiz.why: Profit does not depend on sales alone, but also on the costs of making them.
opts: No, it all depends on its costs
Only if it is listed in the CAC 40

title: Revenue is not profit
examples: A chain selling €10 million of goods but spending €11 million on wages, rent and raw materials is loss-making despite impressive revenue.
LVMH posts both high revenue and a high profit margin: it is the second figure that really reassures investors.
paragraphs: Revenue is everything a company takes in by selling its products. Profit is what is left once all its costs are paid.
A company can post enormous revenue and still lose money if its costs are too high.

quiz.q: What happens when you buy an Nvidia share today?
quiz.why: Except during an IPO, trades happen between investors on the secondary market.
opts: You buy it directly from Nvidia
You buy it from another investor on the secondary market
You take part in its stock market listing

title: Primary market vs secondary market
examples: A company's stock market listing is a rare event; nearly all daily trading happens afterwards, on the secondary market.
Krezus lets you buy and sell on the secondary market, at prices set continuously by supply and demand.
paragraphs: The primary market is when a company sells its shares for the first time (the stock market listing). The secondary market is the trading between investors that follows.
When you buy an Nvidia share today, you buy it from another investor — not from Nvidia itself.

quiz.q: How is market capitalisation calculated?
quiz.why: Market capitalisation reflects the company's total value on the market, not just the price of one share.
opts: Share price × total number of shares

title: What is market capitalisation?
examples: A €900 share with 20 million shares outstanding is worth less in market capitalisation than a €50 share with 2 billion shares.
Nvidia passed $3 trillion in market capitalisation in 2024 — one of the highest valuations ever reached.
paragraphs: Market capitalisation is a company's total value on the stock market: the price of one share multiplied by the total number of shares.
It lets you compare the size of two companies, even when their per-share prices are very different.

quiz.q: What is herd bias?
quiz.why: This bias means acting like the majority, for fear of missing out, rather than on your own analysis.
opts: Following the crowd without thinking for yourself

title: Herd bias
examples: Buying a stock just because it is buzzing on social media, without understanding what the company does, is a classic case of herd bias.
Hercule warns you when your behaviour looks like trend-following rather than a considered decision.
paragraphs: Herd bias pushes you to buy because "everyone is buying", and to sell because "everyone is panicking" — without thinking for yourself.
This behaviour amplifies bubbles and crashes. The calmest investors think against the current.

quiz.q: Why is FOMO risky when investing?
quiz.why: Buying in a hurry after a rise usually means paying the highest price.
opts: It pushes you to buy after a sharp rise, often at the worst moment

title: Fear of missing out (FOMO)
examples: After a 20% rise in a week, buying in a hurry usually means buying at the highest price.
Krezus measures your FOMO score to help you spot these reflexes before you act.
paragraphs: FOMO pushes you to buy urgently after a sharp rise, for fear of "missing the train". That is often the worst moment to invest.
A decision taken in the grip of emotion is rarely a good financial decision.

quiz.q: What should you do about a temporary market fall?
quiz.why: Temporary falls are part of how markets normally work; panic-selling locks in a loss that could have healed.
opts: Stay calm and think long term

title: Accepting losses, a normal day on the market
examples: A stock can lose 3% on a Monday and gain 4% the following Tuesday: reacting to every daily move is rarely useful.
Investors who panic-sold during the falls of 2020 missed the recovery that came a few months later.
paragraphs: A stock that falls on a given day does not mean a bad investment: that is the normal volatility of markets.
Panic-selling after a fall turns a temporary loss into a permanent one.

quiz.q: What is an emergency fund for?
quiz.why: It covers the unexpected without forcing you to liquidate investments, sometimes at the worst possible moment.
opts: Investing more on the stock market
Avoiding having to sell your shares when something unexpected happens

title: Building an emergency fund
examples: An €800 car breakdown should not force you to sell shares in the middle of a market fall.
With €1,500 of monthly spending, an emergency fund would be somewhere between €4,500 and €9,000.
paragraphs: Before investing, it is wise to set aside 3 to 6 months of everyday spending, easy to access.
That cushion means you never have to sell your shares at the wrong moment when something unexpected happens.

quiz.q: Why start investing early, even with small amounts?
quiz.why: The longer you stay invested, the more time compound interest has to do its work.
opts: Time amplifies the effect of compound interest

title: Budget: spend, save, invest
examples: A common rule: 50% essential spending, 30% wants, 20% saving and investing.
Investing €25 a month from age 20 builds a far larger pot than €100 a month from age 35, thanks to time.
paragraphs: A simple rule splits income into three blocks: essential spending, an emergency fund, and long-term investment.
Even small amounts invested regularly make a real difference over ten or twenty years.

quiz.q: Why understand what a company does before investing?
quiz.why: Over time, a share price reflects the real health of the company's business.
opts: It is not necessary, only the price matters
It helps you understand why the price moves

title: What does a listed company actually do?
examples: Nvidia does not "go up" by magic: it sells chips used in artificial intelligence, and demand keeps growing.
Air Liquide never makes headlines, but supplies industrial gases that factories worldwide depend on — a quiet, stable business.
paragraphs: Behind every share sits a real company, with employees, products and customers.
Understanding what a company does before investing tells you why its price might rise — or fall.

quiz.q: Why is it useful to know the sectors?
quiz.why: Knowing the sectors helps you understand why two stocks can react differently to the same news.
opts: They react differently to the same economic events
They are all correlated in the same way

title: Business sectors
examples: Nvidia (technology), LVMH (luxury) and Air Liquide (industry) represent three very different sectors in one portfolio.
When interest rates rise, technology stocks often react more sharply than industrial ones.
paragraphs: Listed companies are grouped into sectors: technology, healthcare, industry, luxury, energy…
Each sector reacts differently to the economy: tech can soar in times of innovation, energy follows commodity prices.

quiz.q: What advantage is often associated with listed family companies?
quiz.why: A founding family, usually a long-term shareholder, tends to favour endurance over quarterly performance.

title: Family companies vs multinationals
examples: LVMH is still run by the Arnault family, its majority shareholder, which encourages a very long-term view.
Other large companies have no dominant family shareholder: decisions there are taken collectively by a board.
paragraphs: Some listed companies are still run by their founding family; others are held by millions of shareholders scattered around the world.
That form of governance sometimes shapes decisions: a family company often thinks in decades, not just about the next quarter.
